I hate multilib. It means installing every library on your system twice. There are so many ways it's buggy and nothing ever seems to work right with it. Most unfortunate the two programs most likely to be used my new users who can't / don't want to figure this stuff out are Wine and Steam. If any two packages should not require multilib support for the sake of improving new user experience it's those two. If a more esoteric package like a mips assembly language simulator needed multilib that would be ok.

The sad thing is with more effort wine does support x86_64. It's just changing one flag when compiling. After we fix that one, there is only one software remaining we need to get on board with 64bit. The steam client.

I say to encourage this we drop multi-lib in general and we tell people if you want to target linux you need to be able to compile to 64. There are more difficult programming tasks necissary to support linux in code that was initially designed for windows. The threads, signals, locks, sockets all require coding specific to linux's kernel. If your code can't support an architecture that has all the same registers and more something is wrong, and that's just if you are in assembly. If you are using c it should compile with no problem to x86_64 unless you are mixing up your integer declaration or something. There is just no excuse. If you can figure out linux system calls you can figure out x86_64.

Let's kill multilib. If you are doing something more esoteric I say we ask those users to compile themselves. Multilib has just acted as a crutch to encourage bad programming. After wine is taken care of then there would only be one major package justifying multilib's existance. That's a lot of inferstructure we don't need and a lot of testing per release of distro.

Are you guy's using multilib for anything else more critical to sysadmins?

Edit: I suppose the reason you can get 64 bit wine if you really want it but not steam is because of access to the source code. Funny how that helps solve problems.
Let's push for reduced need for multilib.

People still use floppy disks.

So, don't hold your breath.
